text: More than 200 years ago, Muhammad Ali, governor of Egypt, set up a printing press near Cairo.
Arab thinkers asked how to learn the knowledge that made Europe powerful without losing their language and faith.
src: Muhammad Ali of Egypt, governor from 1805 / Muhammad Ali founds a government press at Bulaq, near Cairo
how Arabs could acquire the knowledge and techniques that had made Europe powerful without losing their language, faith and identity

text: The Nahda, which means "awakening", was a movement of Arab writers, translators and teachers, Muslim and Christian.
They started newspapers, schools and dictionaries, mostly in Cairo and Beirut.
src: The Nahda, the “awakening”, was a movement of 19th-century Arab writers, translators and teachers, Muslim and Christian
Through printing presses, newspapers, journals, dictionaries, schools and translations, centred in Cairo and Beirut

text: Rifa'a al-Tahtawi went to Paris with Egyptian students and wrote a book about France.
Back in Cairo, he ran a school that trained translators.
src: Rifa’a al-Tahtawi goes to Paris as imam of an Egyptian student mission; his account of France appears in 1834
from 1835 he directed the School of Languages in Cairo, which trained translators

text: Muhammad Abduh taught that Islam, rightly understood, agrees with modern science.
src: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh argued that Islam, rightly understood, was a religion of reason, compatible with modern science

text: Qasim Amin and women writers such as Aisha Taymur called for girls and women to be educated.
But most people in Egypt and Syria could not read, and its ideas reached them only slowly.
src: Qasim Amin and women writers such as Aisha Taymur and Zaynab Fawwaz called for the education of women
most people in Egypt and Syria could not read / its ideals of education reached the poor, the countryside and most women only slowly

text: Jurji Zaydan started the magazine al-Hilal in Cairo, and it went on long after him.
Its plainer Arabic is still used today in books and newspapers across the Arab world.
src: Jurji Zaydan founds al-Hilal in Cairo / some of its journals, al-Hilal among them, long outlived their founders
Its prose is, with changes, the Modern Standard Arabic of books, newspapers and broadcasting across the Arab world / plainer than the ornate style of earlier centuries
